text:
Under a light microscope at a magnification of x400, a cell's image is 12 mm across.
Which of the following could the cell be?
options: a bacterium such as Escherichia coli
solution: Actual size = image size / magnification = 12 mm / 400 = 0.03 mm = 30 micrometres. A liver cell is about 20-30 micrometres. A red blood cell is about 7-8, E. coli about 2, a human egg about 100-120 micrometres, and a virus is far smaller (about 0.1).

text:
Which row is right for neutrophils in a healthy person?

| | produced in the bone marrow | engulf and digest bacteria | release antibodies |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| row 2 | ✓ | x | ✓ |
| row 3 | ✓ | ✓ | x |
| row 4 | x | ✓ | x |
| row 5 | x | x | ✓ |

Key: ✓ yes, x no
solution: Neutrophils, like all white blood cells, are produced in the bone marrow. They are phagocytes: they engulf bacteria and digest them with enzymes from their lysosomes. Antibodies are released by plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes, not by neutrophils. Row 3.

text: Which one of the following happens during metaphase of mitosis in a human skin cell?
options: The nuclear envelope re-forms around each set of chromosomes.
The chromosomes line up at the equator, each attached to spindle fibres from both poles.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange sections.
solution: Metaphase is when the chromosomes sit on the equator of the spindle. The nuclear envelope re-forms in telophase and the cytoplasm divides in cytokinesis; DNA replicates earlier, in the S phase of interphase. Pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over happen only in meiosis.

text:
Which row gives a correct component of each of these cell structures?

| | cell surface membrane | ribosome | chromosome |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | cellulose | DNA | glycogen |
| row 2 | phospholipids | glycogen | RNA |
| row 3 | starch | protein | lipid |
| row 4 | protein | phospholipids | cellulose |
| row 5 | phospholipids | RNA | histone proteins |
solution: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins. A ribosome is made of ribosomal RNA and protein, with no membrane. A eukaryotic chromosome is DNA wound around histone proteins. Cellulose is in plant cell walls, and glycogen and starch are storage carbohydrates. Row 5.

text:
Liver cells and skin cells taken from the same person make different proteins. Assume there are no mutations.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1 The liver cells and the skin cells contain the same genes.
2 The liver cells and the skin cells express different sets of genes.
3 The skin cells have lost the genes that code for liver proteins.
solution: All body cells come from the zygote by mitosis, so they carry the same genes (1). They differ because each cell type switches on a different set of genes (2). Genes are not lost: a skin cell still has the liver genes, just not expressed (3 wrong).

text:
Which of the following is/are organs?
1 the stomach
2 blood
3 the skin
solution: An organ is made of several tissues working together. The stomach has muscle, epithelium, glandular and nervous tissue; the skin has epithelium, connective tissue, blood vessels and nerves, and is the body's largest organ. Blood is a single (connective) tissue. So 1 and 3 only.

text:
The same short section of a gene is read from two individuals, P and Q:
P TACGGATTC
Q TACGAATTC
Which single mutation explains the difference between P and Q?
options: addition of an A after the fourth base
substitution of G by A at the fifth base
inversion of the fourth to sixth bases
substitution of C by A at the third base
solution: Both are nine bases long, so nothing was added or removed. Comparing base by base, they differ only at position 5: G in P, A in Q. That is a substitution. A deletion or addition would change the length, and inverting GGA would give AGG at positions 4-6.

text:
Cubes of beetroot are washed to remove the red pigment released from cells damaged by cutting. One cube is then put into water at 20 °C and another into water at 70 °C for ten minutes.
Which row shows the expected results and their explanation?

| | water at 20 °C | water at 70 °C | explanation for the water at 70 °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | turns red | stays clear | heat destroys the pigment |
| row 2 | stays clear | stays clear | heat makes the membrane less permeable |
| row 3 | turns red | turns red | the pigment diffuses through intact membranes |
| row 4 | stays clear | turns red | membrane proteins denature and the membrane becomes leaky |
| row 5 | stays clear | turns red | phospholipids dissolve in hot water |
solution: At 20 °C intact membranes hold the pigment in, so the water stays clear. At 70 °C the membrane proteins denature and the bilayer is disrupted, leaving gaps the pigment escapes through, so the water turns red. Phospholipids do not dissolve in water at any temperature, so row 5 has the right result but the wrong reason. Row 4.

text:
Which of the following rows are correct?

| | molecule | contains nitrogen | contains phosphorus |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | ALL nucleotides | yes | yes |
| row 2 | glucose | no | no |
| row 3 | a triglyceride | no | no |
| row 4 | ALL monosaccharides | yes | no |
solution: A nucleotide is a phosphate, a sugar and a nitrogenous base, so it has both N and P. Glucose and triglycerides are built from C, H and O only. Monosaccharides are too, so row 4 is wrong to say they contain nitrogen. Rows 1, 2 and 3.

text:
When a skeletal muscle fibre contracts, which of the following become shorter?
1 the sarcomeres
2 the actin filaments
3 the myosin filaments
solution: In the sliding filament model, myosin heads pull the actin filaments in towards the centre of each sarcomere. The filaments slide past each other but keep their own lengths; only the overlap increases, so each sarcomere shortens. 1 only.

text:
Which of the following statements about oxygen in a green plant is/are correct?
1 The plant uses oxygen for respiration during the day.
2 The plant releases oxygen from photosynthesis during the night.
3 Some of the oxygen made in photosynthesis can be used by the plant's own mitochondria.
solution: Plant cells respire all the time, day and night, so they use oxygen during the day too (1). Photosynthesis needs light, so no oxygen is made at night (2 wrong). Oxygen released in the chloroplasts can diffuse straight to the mitochondria of the same cell (3). So 1 and 3 only.

text:
A gene is inserted into a bacterial plasmid to make recombinant DNA.
Which statement about this process is correct?
options: DNA ligase breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the sticky ends together.
Restriction enzymes join the gene to the plasmid.
DNA ligase makes phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Reverse transcriptase copies the plasmid into mRNA.
The plasmid and the gene must be cut with different restriction enzymes.
solution: A restriction enzyme cuts both the plasmid and the gene, and using the SAME enzyme gives matching sticky ends. The sticky ends pair by hydrogen bonds, and DNA ligase then seals the backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template.

text:
A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Starting from one cell, how many cells are there after 3 hours?
[Assume every cell survives and keeps dividing.]
solution: 3 hours is 180 minutes, which is 9 division times of 20 minutes. Each division doubles the number, so after 9 divisions there are \(2^9 = 512\) cells. 9 counts the divisions, not the cells.

text: Which statement about oxygen transport in healthy humans is correct?
options: Fetal haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin.
Most of the oxygen in blood is carried dissolved in the plasma.
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin less strongly than oxygen does.
At high altitude haemoglobin is fully saturated more easily than at sea level.
A rise in temperature in working muscle helps haemoglobin release oxygen there.
solution: Warmth, carbon dioxide and acidity in active muscle lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it unloads more where it is needed. Fetal haemoglobin has a HIGHER affinity, to take oxygen from the mother's blood. Almost all oxygen rides on haemoglobin, carbon monoxide binds far more strongly than oxygen, and the low partial pressure at altitude makes saturation harder.

text:
Which of the following processes use ATP?
1 pumping sodium ions out of a nerve cell
2 contraction of a muscle
3 diffusion of oxygen from an alveolus into the blood
4 the Calvin cycle in a chloroplast
solution: The sodium-potassium pump is active transport and uses ATP. Myosin heads use ATP to detach from actin and re-cock. The Calvin cycle uses ATP (and NADPH) from the light-dependent reactions to make sugar. Diffusion is passive, down a concentration gradient, and needs no ATP. So 1, 2 and 4.

chapter: States of Matter and Gas Laws
text:
Salt is spread on an icy road at -3 °C and the ice melts, although the air stays at -3 °C.
Which of the following statements explain(s) this?
1 The salt raises the temperature of the ice.
2 Salt water has a lower freezing point than pure water.
3 Dissolving salt makes the water molecules move more slowly.
solution: A dissolved solute lowers the freezing point of water, here below -3 °C, so at -3 °C the salty water is above its freezing point and the ice melts. The salt does not heat anything (melting actually takes energy from the surroundings), and the temperature, not the solute, sets the molecules' average speed. 2 only.

text:
In which of these reactions does at least one element change its oxidation number?
1 \(\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}\)
2 \(\mathrm{2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2}\)
3 \(\mathrm{AgNO_3 + NaCl \rightarrow AgCl + NaNO_3}\)
solution: Check oxidation numbers. In 1, Ca stays +2, C +4 and O -2: no change. In 2, oxygen starts at -1 in hydrogen peroxide and ends at -2 in water and 0 in oxygen: it is both reduced and oxidised (disproportionation), so it is redox. In 3, every element keeps its oxidation number: a precipitation. 2 only.

text:
Hydrogen and iodine react in a sealed vessel of volume V:
\(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\)
At equilibrium the vessel contains 0.20 mol of \(\mathrm{H_2}\), 0.10 mol of \(\mathrm{I_2}\) and 0.80 mol of HI.
What is \(K_c\) at this temperature?
solution: \(K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]}\). Each concentration is moles / V, and with two moles of gas on each side the V terms cancel: \(K_c = \dfrac{0.80^2}{0.20 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{0.64}{0.020} = 32\). Forgetting to square [HI] gives 40.

text:
A compound contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. 9.0 g of it contains 3.6 g of carbon and 0.6 g of hydrogen.
Which one of the following could be its molecular formula?
[Relative atomic masses: C = 12; H = 1; O = 16]
solution: Oxygen = 9.0 - 3.6 - 0.6 = 4.8 g. Moles: C 3.6/12 = 0.30, H 0.6/1 = 0.60, O 4.8/16 = 0.30. The ratio 1 : 2 : 1 gives the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\), so the molecular formula is a multiple of it: \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\) (ethanoic acid) fits.

text: Why does propane, \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\), boil at a higher temperature than ethane, \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\)?
options: Propane molecules have more electrons, so the London (dispersion) forces between them are stronger.
The carbon-carbon bonds in propane are stronger than the one in ethane.
Propane molecules hydrogen-bond to each other but ethane molecules do not.
Propane has permanent dipole forces between its molecules but ethane does not.
Boiling propane breaks covalent bonds, which takes more energy.
solution: Both are non-polar alkanes, so only London forces act between their molecules. Propane is larger with more electrons, giving stronger instantaneous dipoles and more contact between molecules. Boiling separates molecules; it never breaks the covalent bonds inside them, and neither alkane has hydrogen bonds or permanent dipoles worth counting.

text:
Element W is a soft, shiny solid that reacts vigorously with cold water, releasing hydrogen. Its oxide has the formula \(\mathrm{W_2O}\) and dissolves in water to give an alkaline solution.
Which family of elements does W belong to?
solution: The formula (mathrm{W_2O}) means W forms (mathrm{W^+}) ions: two of them balance one (mathrm{O^{2-}}). A soft metal that reacts vigorously with cold water and has a basic oxide is an alkali metal (Group 1). An alkaline earth metal would form WO.

text: Why does a chloride ion have a charge of -1?
options: It has one more proton than it has electrons.
It has one more neutron than it has protons.
It has one more electron than it has protons.
It has the same number of electrons as protons.
solution: Charge is protons (+) minus electrons (-); neutrons carry no charge. A chlorine atom (17 protons, 17 electrons) gains one electron to become \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) with 18 electrons, one more than its protons. Losing an electron would make a positive ion.

text:
Which of these molecules are polar overall?
1 \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\)
2 \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\)
3 \(\mathrm{HCl}\)
solution: Tetrachloromethane is a symmetrical tetrahedron with four identical C-Cl bonds, so the bond dipoles cancel. In trichloromethane one position holds an H instead of Cl, so the dipoles no longer cancel. HCl has a single polar bond. 2 and 3 only.

text:
Phenolphthalein is put into a flask of dilute HCl, and NaOH(aq) is run in from a burette until the base is in excess.
What does the indicator do?
solution: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and neutral solutions and pink above about pH 8-10. The flask starts acidic (colourless). After 25 mL the acid is neutralised, and the extra 10 mL leaves the solution alkaline, so it turns pink. Red and yellow are colours of other indicators, such as methyl orange.

text:
A sample of chlorine contains three atoms of chlorine-35 for every one atom of chlorine-37.
What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine in this sample?
solution: Weight each isotope by its share: \((3 \times 35 + 1 \times 37)/4 = 142/4 = 35.5\). The simple average of 35 and 37 (36.0) ignores that chlorine-35 is three times as common; 71 is the relative molecular mass of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).

text:
Which of the following pairs are structural isomers?
1 \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\)
2 \(\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}\)
3 \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)
solution: Count the atoms. Pair 1: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, both \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\). Pair 2: methyl ethanoate and propanoic acid, both \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O_2}\). Pair 3: propanal and propanone, both \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O}\). Each pair has one formula but different structures, so all three.

text:
What mass of sodium carbonate, \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\), is needed to make 250 mL of a 0.20 mol/L solution?
[Relative atomic masses: C = 12; O = 16; Na = 23]
solution: Moles needed = 0.250 L x 0.20 mol/L = 0.050 mol. \(M_r\) of \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) = 46 + 12 + 48 = 106. Mass = 0.050 x 106 = 5.3 g. Using 250 instead of 0.250 L, or forgetting the second Na, gives the wrong options.

subject: Physics
text:
A train starts from rest and speeds up uniformly at 0.50 m/s² for 40 s. It then travels at a steady speed for 2.0 minutes.
What is its top speed, and how far does it go during the steady-speed part?
solution: Top speed \(v = at = 0.50 \times 40 = 20\) m/s. The steady part lasts 120 s, so it covers \(20 \times 120 = 2400\) m. 400 m is the speeding-up part (\(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 40\)) and 2800 m the whole journey.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Three parcels have a mean mass of 4.0 kg. The heaviest is 5.5 kg and the range of their masses is 2.5 kg.
What is the median mass?
solution: The lightest is 5.5 - 2.5 = 3.0 kg. The three add up to 3 x 4.0 = 12 kg, so the middle parcel is 12 - 5.5 - 3.0 = 3.5 kg, which is the median. Here the median is below the mean, because the heaviest parcel pulls the mean up.

subject: Physics
text:
A metal block of volume \(500\ \text{cm}^3\) and density \(2.70\ \text{g/cm}^3\) hangs on a string, fully under water of density \(1.00\ \text{g/cm}^3\).
What is the tension in the string?
[Take \(g = 10\) N/kg.]
solution: Mass = 500 x 2.70 = 1350 g = 1.35 kg, so weight = 13.5 N. The block displaces 500 cm3 of water, mass 0.500 kg, so the upthrust is 5.0 N. The string holds the rest: 13.5 - 5.0 = 8.5 N.

subject: Physics
text:
The volume of a sample of an ideal gas is measured at several temperatures while its pressure is kept constant. Volume (y-axis) is plotted against temperature in degrees Celsius (x-axis).
Which description fits the graph?
options: a straight line through the origin
a straight line with positive gradient that would meet the temperature axis at about -273 °C
a curve whose gradient decreases as temperature rises
a straight line with negative gradient
solution: At constant pressure V is proportional to the ABSOLUTE temperature, \(T = \theta + 273\). Against Celsius that is still a straight line with positive gradient, but shifted: it reaches zero volume at \(\theta = -273\) °C, absolute zero. It would pass through the origin only if plotted against kelvin.

subject: Mathematics
text: What is the lowest common multiple of 12, 18 and 30, written as a product of powers of primes?
solution: \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\). The LCM takes the HIGHEST power of each prime: \(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180\). Taking the lowest powers gives the HCF, \(2 \times 3 = 6\).

subject: Mathematics
text:
The equation \(\dfrac{2}{x} + \dfrac{3}{x+1} = 2\), with \(x \ne 0\) and \(x \ne -1\), has two real solutions.
What do they add up to?
solution: Multiply through by \(x(x+1)\): \(2(x+1) + 3x = 2x(x+1)\), so \(5x + 2 = 2x^2 + 2x\) and \(2x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0\). This factorises as \((2x+1)(x-2) = 0\): \(x = 2\) or \(x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), which add up to 1.5 (as \(-b/a = 3/2\) also shows).

subject: Mathematics
text: For every integer \(n\), \(\dfrac{27^{n} \times 9^{2n}}{3^{n}}\) is equal to:
solution: Write each as a power of 3: \(27^n = 3^{3n}\) and \(9^{2n} = 3^{4n}\). Multiplying adds the indices and dividing subtracts: \(3n + 4n - n = 6n\). Forgetting to divide by \(3^n\) gives \(3^{7n}\).

subject: Physics
text:
Two small charged spheres 30 cm apart repel each other with a force F. The charge on one sphere is doubled, the charge on the other is halved, and they are moved to 10 cm apart.
What is the force between them now?
solution: Coulomb's law: \(F \propto \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\). Doubling one charge and halving the other leaves the product unchanged. The distance falls to a third, so \(r^2\) falls to a ninth and the force rises nine times: 9F.
